chapter: Union, Emmett Hardy and Rampart Street Parade
title: Union membership and who played in New Orleans theatres
summary: Jazz players were union members, and the theatre pit men and small five-piece bands are described; a reading test was needed.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I just wanted to, we didn't have the machine on before. Yeah. And, uh, when your father was in the union, what kind of musicians were in the union then? Were they?

Well, the Spora band, you remember when you saw the picture of the Spora band? Mm-hmm. Well, he, he played, played out at the parks and stuff like that, see? Yeah. And then, uh, of course, I know, I didn't know him, I mean, I didn't know who was in the band at the, at the, at the French Opera House when he played C Cornette. Yeah. But, uh, that was before I was born, I think. Mm-hmm. Or something like that. I, I don't remember too much about them. No. I was too young. Well. Before I had, had any idea of, of even playing, uh, having a fast sticks in my hand, see?
Well, I just wondered if they let the jazz musicians in the union, if they had any trouble getting in.

Well, they had to, had to have, uh, jazz musicians. I mean, it wasn't a matter of, uh, of what style you played in, in, in any union down there. Mm-hmm. You know what I mean? I mean, as far as, as far as the musicians' union. Yeah. I mean, uh, because, all the guys that played in the theater in the pits. Mm-hmm. You know, all those theaters that I had in, like the Crescent and, and, and, and, uh, and the Opium Theater, and,
and, uh, Palace Theater, and, uh, everybody, everybody that, that, uh, that played in theaters, they're all union musicians. Mm-hmm.

And, uh, they didn't, didn't say, well, geez, are you a jazz man or what? Uh, point out what you, what you do? I mean, it's up to the guys, uh, to find out, uh, after, after you play, whatever you do, you know? Yeah. You know, whatever, you thought you could play some jazz? So, so that, that's when, uh, when Tony Perani had his band, they were playing at the, at the, at the Greenwald Grill downstairs, see? Mm-hmm. I don't know what it was, Johnny Bison, uh, Johnny Detroit's band down there first, and, uh, Santo was playing, I took trombone down there, and then, then, then, then moved over to Cobb, see? Mm-hmm. And there was two or three different places that, that had the little bands like that, but there were only five, five piece bands, and sometimes, when, when, when, when the boss was giving up money, they'd have a bass player in there, see? Mm-hmm. So the majority of the thing was more on a pattern of a Dixieland band, like, like, like the original Dixieland jazz band, see? Five men.
Did the, did you have to have a test to get in the Union, in those days?
